headline: Speed Cameras Caught Lying; Nation's Drivers Declared Retroactively Innocent
subheadline: *Home Office revokes cameras' licence to snitch, instantly transforming thousands of convicted speeders into misunderstood victims of flawed photography.*
author: Marjorie Bunting, Motoring Grievance Desk
seoTitle: Speed Cameras Caught Lying, Drivers Vindicated | The Daily Absurd
seoDescription: Satire: the Home Office has withdrawn approval for speed camera evidence, retroactively converting Britain's fined motorists into wronged folk heroes.
sourceEvent: The Home Office has revoked the approval that allowed footage from certain speed cameras to be used as evidence, after a fault raised doubts about the reliability of the recordings. The move means some drivers who were caught speeding may have escaped fines they would otherwise have received.

social.x: BREAKING: The Home Office has revoked speed cameras' licence to snitch. Thousands of British motorists have been retroactively reclassified from 'offenders' to 'people who were right all along, actually'.
social.facebook: Britain's speed cameras have had their evidence thrown out for being unreliable, which means every argument you had with a yellow box on the A414 has now been won. Retroactively. Our Motoring Grievance Desk reports on the nation's newly minted victims of flawed photography.
social.linkedin: A recent evidentiary review has determined that thousands of recorded speeding incidents cannot be relied upon, effectively converting a fixed penalty backlog into a fixed apology backlog. Stakeholders are advised to drive normally, which in Britain means 'with grievance'.
social.instagram: Turns out the speed camera was lying and you, doing 38 in a 30, were simply 'ahead of your time'. All fines may be redeemed for one (1) smug nod. #satire #speedcamera #britain
altHeadlines: Yellow Box on A41 Issues Formal Apology to Everyone It Has Ever Judged
Nation's Gloveboxes Declare Amnesty, Return Three Years of Unpaid Fines as 'Keepsakes'

body:
The Home Office has withdrawn its approval for speed camera footage to be used as evidence, after discovering that the devices had been — in the words of one official — 'a bit liberal with the truth, speed-wise'.

The ruling instantly reclassified thousands of Britain's most convicted motorists from 'dangerous offenders' to 'victims of flawed photography', a legal status previously held only by people who looked bad in their passport photo.

Across the country, drivers who once muttered 'I was barely over the limit' while paying a £100 fine have been vindicated in the strongest possible terms: a government form. Several have already contacted their local constabulary to ask whether the apology will arrive by post or, fittingly, by recorded delivery.

"I always said that camera had it in for me," said local man Derek Phelps, 52, who was photographed doing 36 in a 30 zone outside a petrol station in 2023. "Turns out I was doing 29 with intent. I've framed the penalty notice. It's a portrait of injustice now."

A spokesperson for an unnamed motoring organisation welcomed the news, calling it 'a landmark moment for people who have definitely never broken the speed limit and are furious about being accused of it'.

The fallout has extended beyond the roadside. Insurance companies are reportedly reviewing premiums charged to drivers penalised on the strength of 'a Polaroid taken by a vending machine'. One analyst described the affected camera network as 'essentially a line of unpaid tabloid photographers with delusions of judiciary'.

Meanwhile, the cameras themselves face an uncertain future. Some units have been quietly switched off; others remain in place, flashing at passing cars 'more as a suggestion now'. One decommissioned unit on the outskirts of Swindon was seen being carried away by two contractors while a small crowd of motorists gathered to point, the way people point at a famous actor.

Legal experts caution that the ruling does not technically mean anyone was innocent, only that the evidence was unreliable — a distinction the nation's drivers have unanimously voted to ignore.

"The state cannot prove I was speeding," said one woman in Reading, reversing out of a tight space and clipping a bollard, "and therefore I have never been speeding, and frankly the road owes me a letter."

At press time, the Home Office was said to be reviewing the evidentiary status of parking wardens, who were last seen insisting they 'witnessed it themselves', which is apparently no longer enough.
